scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Yanvalou originates from the Fon and Mahi peoples of present-day Benin, West Africa, and was brought to Haiti as part of the Vodou tradition.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Yanvalou is performed during Rada rituals to honor the lwa Damballah (serpent spirit of fertility) and Agwé (deity of the sea).
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by a low center of gravity with bent knees.
The primary movement is a spinal undulation that flows from the head to the pelvis, often with hands placed on the knees.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The rhythm is played on a set of three percussion instruments: the maman, the seconde (or segun), and the boula (or bass) drums, accompanied by an ogan (iron bell).
Listen for the maman drum, seconde drum, boula drum, ogan.
A slow, percussive ensemble featuring three drums of varying sizes and a metallic iron bell, creating a steady, wave-like pulse.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Variations include Yanvalou Fran (base), Yanvalou debout (standing), Yanvalou des bas (squatting), Yanvalou z'epaules (shoulder dance), Yanvalou Gede (for the Festival of the Dead), and Yanvalou Maskowan (advanced).
Derived from the Fon and Mahi peoples of Benin.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Rada is shares music of Banda: Yanvalou Gede is a slower version of the Banda rhythm.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Yanvalou is a sacred dance performed during Rada rituals to honor specific lwa; outsiders should approach with respect for its religious significance.
